782.04.title: Murder

rows.trigger: Premeditated design to effect the death of the person killed or any human being. NO DOLLAR VALUE IS AN ELEMENT ANYWHERE IN THIS SECTION: min and max are null because value is not a trigger at all, not because a bound is missing. The degree is assigned by flush language at the end of paragraph (1)(a), which attaches equally to subparagraphs 1., 2., and 3. -- reading only subparagraph 1. would miss two entirely separate routes to a capital felony. Level is null: the only 921.0022 entry keyed to 782.04(1) is the Level 9 line 'Attempt, conspire, or solicit to commit premeditated murder,' which is the inchoate offense, not the completed murder; completed capital felonies are not ranked on the chart.
rows.quote: The unlawful killing of a human being: 1. When perpetrated from a premeditated design to effect the death of the person killed or any human being; . . . is murder in the first degree and constitutes a capital felony, punishable as provided in s. 775.082.

rows.trigger: Felony murder: killing committed by a person engaged in the perpetration of, or attempt to perpetrate, any of the nineteen enumerated predicates in sub-subparagraphs a. through s. No premeditation required. No dollar value is an element, so min and max are null. Note sub-subparagraph s. (human trafficking) appears in the (1)(a)2. list but has NO counterpart in the subsection (3) list and NO counterpart in the subsection (4) exclusion list -- the three enumerated lists in this section are not identical and must each be read in full. Level null: capital felonies are not ranked in the 921.0022 chart.
rows.quote: 2. When committed by a person engaged in the perpetration of, or in the attempt to perpetrate, any: a. Trafficking offense prohibited by s. 893.135(1), b. Arson, c. Sexual battery, d. Robbery, e. Burglary, f. Kidnapping, g. Escape, h. Aggravated child abuse, i. Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult, j. Aircraft piracy, k. Unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb, l. Carjacking, m. Home-invasion robbery, n. Aggravated stalking, o. Murder of another human being, p. Resisting an officer with violence to his or her person, q. Aggravated fleeing or eluding with serious bodily injury or death, r. Felony that is an act of terrorism or is in furtherance of an act of terrorism, including a felony under s. 775.30, s. 775.32, s. 775.33, s. 775.34, or s. 775.35, or s. Human trafficking; or . . . is murder in the first degree and constitutes a capital felony, punishable as provided in s. 775.082.

rows.trigger: Drug-delivery murder: death resulting from unlawful distribution BY A PERSON 18 YEARS OF AGE OR OLDER of any substance listed in sub-subparagraphs a.-j. (schedule I substances, cocaine, opium and its salts/derivatives, methadone, alfentanil, carfentanil, fentanyl, sufentanil, methamphetamine, and analogs of any of these), or a mixture containing one, where the substance or mixture is proven to have caused, or to have been a substantial factor in producing, the death of the user. 'Substantial factor' is defined in subsection (6)(a). No dollar value and no drug-weight threshold is an element, so min and max are null. Level null: capital felonies are not ranked in the 921.0022 chart. CORRECTED -- DO NOT SAY THAT AN UNDER-18 DISTRIBUTOR SIMPLY FALLS UNDER (5)(b). Age 18+ is an element of this subparagraph, but (5)(b) is NOT a general under-18 mirror of it. (5)(b) reaches only substances the distributor knew or should have known contained 'dangerous fentanyl or fentanyl analogs,' which (5)(a)1. defines by reference to s. 893.135(1)(c)4.a.(I)-(VII) -- far narrower than the a.-j. list here. A person under 18 who distributes cocaine, opium, methadone, or methamphetamine causing death is outside (5)(b) entirely; that conduct is not removed from subsection (4) either, because exclusion (4)(l) strips out only 'Unlawful distribution ... by a person 18 years of age or older.' It therefore lands in (4), third degree murder, a second degree felony at severity Level 8. The felony degree coincides with (5)(b) but the governing provision and the severity level do not: (4) is Level 8, (5)(b) is unranked.
rows.quote: 3. Which resulted from the unlawful distribution by a person 18 years of age or older of any of the following substances, or mixture containing any of the following substances, when such substance or mixture is proven to have caused, or is proven to have been a substantial factor in producing, the death of the user: a. A substance controlled under s. 893.03(1); b. Cocaine, as described in s. 893.03(2)(a)4.; c. Opium or any synthetic or natural salt, compound, derivative, or preparation of opium; d. Methadone; e. Alfentanil, as described in s. 893.03(2)(b)1.; f. Carfentanil, as described in s. 893.03(2)(b)6.; g. Fentanyl, as described in s. 893.03(2)(b)9.; h. Sufentanil, as described in s. 893.03(2)(b)30.; i. Methamphetamine, as described in s. 893.03(2)(c)5.; or j. A controlled substance analog, as described in s. 893.0356, of any substance specified in sub-subparagraphs a.-i., is murder in the first degree and constitutes a capital felony, punishable as provided in s. 775.082.

rows.trigger: Procedural, not a grading provision: it assigns no degree of offense. Recorded so the table shows the whole of subsection (1) was read. It fixes the capital sentencing procedure (s. 921.141) that decides death versus life imprisonment, and imposes a 45-day post-arraignment deadline for the state's notice of intent to seek death, with a required list of aggravating factors and leave to amend for good cause.
rows.quote: (b) In all cases under this section, the procedure set forth in s. 921.141 shall be followed in order to determine sentence of death or life imprisonment. If the prosecutor intends to seek the death penalty, the prosecutor must give notice to the defendant and file the notice with the court within 45 days after arraignment. The notice must contain a list of the aggravating factors the state intends to prove and has reason to believe it can prove beyond a reasonable doubt. The court may allow the prosecutor to amend the notice upon a showing of good cause.

rows.trigger: Depraved-mind second degree murder: an act imminently dangerous to another evincing a depraved mind regardless of human life, WITHOUT premeditated design to effect the death of any particular individual. No dollar value is an element, so min and max are null. Punishment is enhanced above an ordinary first degree felony: 'imprisonment for a term of years not exceeding life.' Level 10 verified by me against the F.S. 921.0022 chart, LEVEL 10 block, entry '782.04(2) | 1st,PBL | Unlawful killing of human; act is homicide, unpremeditated.'
rows.quote: (2) The unlawful killing of a human being, when perpetrated by any act imminently dangerous to another and evincing a depraved mind regardless of human life, although without any premeditated design to effect the death of any particular individual, is murder in the second degree and constitutes a felony of the first degree, punishable by imprisonment for a term of years not exceeding life or as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: Agency-rule felony murder: the killing is done BY A PERSON OTHER THAN the person engaged in the perpetration of or attempt to perpetrate one of the eighteen enumerated felonies in paragraphs (a) through (r); the felony perpetrator is the one who commits second degree murder. This list differs from the (1)(a)2. list -- it omits human trafficking -- so it cannot be assumed identical. No dollar value is an element, so min and max are null. Punishment enhanced: 'imprisonment for a term of years not exceeding life.' Level 9 verified by me against the F.S. 921.0022 chart, LEVEL 9 block, entry '782.04(3) | 1st,PBL | Accomplice to murder in connection with arson, sexual battery, robbery, burglary, aggravated fleeing or eluding with serious bodily injury or death, and other specified felonies.'
rows.quote: (3) When a human being is killed during the perpetration of, or during the attempt to perpetrate, any: (a) Trafficking offense prohibited by s. 893.135(1), (b) Arson, (c) Sexual battery, (d) Robbery, (e) Burglary, (f) Kidnapping, (g) Escape, (h) Aggravated child abuse, (i) Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult, (j) Aircraft piracy, (k) Unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb, (l) Carjacking, (m) Home-invasion robbery, (n) Aggravated stalking, (o) Murder of another human being, (p) Aggravated fleeing or eluding with serious bodily injury or death, (q) Resisting an officer with violence to his or her person, or (r) Felony that is an act of terrorism or is in furtherance of an act of terrorism, including a felony under s. 775.30, s. 775.32, s. 775.33, s. 775.34, or s. 775.35, by a person other than the person engaged in the perpetration of or in the attempt to perpetrate such felony, the person perpetrating or attempting to perpetrate such felony commits murder in the second degree, which constitutes a felony of the first degree, punishable by imprisonment for a term of years not exceeding life or as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: Third degree murder: killing without any design to effect death, by a person engaged in the perpetration of or attempt to perpetrate any felony OTHER THAN the nineteen listed in paragraphs (a) through (s). This is an EXCLUSION list, not an inclusion list -- the listed felonies push the conduct up into (1)(a)2. or (3); every other felony falls here. The nineteen items are not the same nineteen as in (1)(a)2.: this list adds (l) adult drug distribution and omits human trafficking. Paragraph (l) is a trap for the reader: it excludes distribution of the (1)(a)3.a.-j. substances only when done by a person 18 or older, which is why an ADULT drug-delivery death is capital and not third degree murder, and equally why an UNDER-18 distributor of a listed substance that is not dangerous fentanyl or a fentanyl analog stays inside subsection (4) rather than moving to (5)(b). No dollar value is an element, so min and max are null. Level 8 verified by me against the F.S. 921.0022 chart, LEVEL 8 block, entry '782.04(4) | 2nd | Killing of human without design when engaged in act or attempt of any felony other than arson, sexual battery, robbery, burglary, kidnapping, aggravated fleeing or eluding with serious bodily injury or death, aircraft piracy, or unlawfully discharging bomb.'
rows.quote: (4) The unlawful killing of a human being, when perpetrated without any design to effect death, by a person engaged in the perpetration of, or in the attempt to perpetrate, any felony other than any: (a) Trafficking offense prohibited by s. 893.135(1), (b) Arson, (c) Sexual battery, (d) Robbery, (e) Burglary, (f) Kidnapping, (g) Escape, (h) Aggravated child abuse, (i) Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult, (j) Aircraft piracy, (k) Unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb, (l) Unlawful distribution of any substance listed in sub-subparagraphs (1)(a)3.a.-j. by a person 18 years of age or older, when such substance is proven to have caused, or is proven to have been a substantial factor in producing, the death of the user, (m) Carjacking, (n) Home-invasion robbery, (o) Aggravated stalking, (p) Murder of another human being, (q) Aggravated fleeing or eluding with serious bodily injury or death, (r) Resisting an officer with violence to his or her person, or (s) Felony that is an act of terrorism or is in furtherance of an act of terrorism, including a felony under s. 775.30, s. 775.32, s. 775.33, s. 775.34, or s. 775.35, is murder in the third degree and constitutes a felony of the second degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: Juvenile fentanyl-delivery murder: killing without any design to effect death resulting from unlawful distribution BY A PERSON LESS THAN 18 YEARS OF AGE of any substance or mixture that he or she KNEW OR REASONABLY SHOULD HAVE KNOWN contained dangerous fentanyl or fentanyl analogs, proven to have caused or to have been a substantial factor in producing the death of the user. This row also covers the definitions in (5)(a), quoted below: (5)(a)1. 'Dangerous fentanyl or fentanyl analogs' (s. 893.135(1)(c)4.a.(I)-(VII)) and (5)(a)2. 'Distribute' (s. 893.02); (5)(a) assigns no degree of its own. This is NOT a full under-18 mirror of (1)(a)3.: it is narrower in substance (fentanyl and fentanyl analogs only, not the whole a.-j. list) and it adds a scienter element that (1)(a)3. does not state. An under-18 distributor of a non-fentanyl listed substance is charged under (4), not here. No dollar value and no drug-weight threshold is an element, so min and max are null. Level is null and this is a genuine gap, not an oversight: I scanned the entire F.S. 921.0022 chart text for '782.04' and the left column contains exactly four entries -- 782.04(1), (2), (3), and (4). Subsection (5) is UNRANKED in the chart. I did not read s. 921.0023, so I am not inferring a default level, and null must not be read as 'no level applies at sentencing.'
rows.quote: (5)(a) As used in this subsection, the term: 1. "Dangerous fentanyl or fentanyl analogs" means any controlled substance described in s. 893.135(1)(c)4.a.(I)-(VII). 2. "Distribute" has the same meaning as in s. 893.02. (b) The unlawful killing of a human being, when perpetrated without any design to effect death, which resulted from the unlawful distribution by a person less than 18 years of age of any substance or mixture that he or she knew or reasonably should have known contained dangerous fentanyl or fentanyl analogs when such substance or mixture is proven to have caused, or is proven to have been a substantial factor in producing, the death of the user, is murder in the third degree and constitutes a felony of the second degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: Definitional, not a grading provision: it assigns no degree of offense. Recorded so the table's coverage convention holds across the whole section (the same convention that produced the (1)(b) row), and because both definitions are load-bearing elsewhere in the section. (6)(a) 'Substantial factor' supplies the causation element used in (1)(a)3., (4)(l), and (5)(b), and it is broader than but-for causation: the substance alone need only be sufficient to cause death, regardless of whether another substance was also sufficient. (6)(b) 'Terrorism' supplies the predicate used in (1)(a)2.r., (3)(r), and (4)(s), and requires BOTH a qualifying act under subparagraph 1. (a violent act or act dangerous to human life violating state or federal criminal law, OR a violation of s. 815.06) AND one of the three intents in subparagraph 2. The two subparagraphs are joined by 'and,' so neither alone suffices.
rows.quote: (6) As used in this section, the term: (a) "Substantial factor" means that the use of the substance or mixture alone is sufficient to cause death, regardless of whether any other substance or mixture used is also sufficient to cause death. (b) "Terrorism" means an activity that: 1.a. Involves a violent act or an act dangerous to human life which is a violation of the criminal laws of this state or of the United States; or b. Involves a violation of s. 815.06; and 2. Is intended to: a. Intimidate, injure, or coerce a civilian population; b. Influence the policy of a government by intimidation or coercion; or c. Affect the conduct of government through destruction of property, assassination, murder, kidnapping, or aircraft piracy.

rows.trigger: SECTION-LEVEL READING NOTE (moved here from the 775.083(1)(a) row, where it was misplaced -- it is a section-wide caveat, not a life-felony caveat). s. 775.083 assigns NO degree of offense anywhere. It is a fine-cap and cost schedule that CONSUMES degrees assigned by other statutes. The dollar figures in subsection (1) are maximum FINES, not value thresholds that grade an offense, so min/max are null on every row in this table. Never cite this section as the source of an offense degree.

THE STRUCTURAL TRAP IN THIS SECTION, AND THE ONE THE PRIOR TABLE FELL INTO. Subsection (1) is not just the lettered ladder. Unnumbered operative text sits ABOVE paragraph (a) and governs everything below it. It does three things that appear nowhere in (a) through (g): (1) it limits the entire fine authorization to 'an offense other than a capital felony'; (2) it distinguishes a fine IN ADDITION TO s. 775.082 punishment (the default) from a fine IN LIEU OF that punishment (only 'when specifically authorized by statute'); and (3) it separately authorizes a fine for a noncriminal violation. A reader who opens subsection (1), scrolls to the lettered tier matching the degree they came for, and stops will miss all three. Each is broken out as its own row below.
rows.quote: A person who has been convicted of an offense other than a capital felony may be sentenced to pay a fine in addition to any punishment described in s. 775.082; when specifically authorized by statute, he or she may be sentenced to pay a fine in lieu of any punishment described in s. 775.082. A person who has been convicted of a noncriminal violation may be sentenced to pay a fine. Fines for designated crimes and for noncriminal violations shall not exceed:

rows.cite: 775.083(1) (introductory text, first clause -- capital felony exclusion)
rows.degree: capital felony -- EXCLUDED from this section's fine authorization
rows.trigger: CAPITAL FELONY CARVE-OUT. The (a) through (e) ladder runs life felony, first/second degree felony, third degree felony, first degree misdemeanor, and second degree misdemeanor/noncriminal violation. Capital felony is absent from that ladder NOT by drafting oversight but because this lead-in clause excludes it: the fine authority reaches only 'an offense other than a capital felony.' Do not read the table's silence as 'uncapped' or 'not yet entered.' A capital felony is outside s. 775.083(1) fine authorization entirely. Note the asymmetry against paragraph (a): a LIFE felony is inside the section and capped at $15,000; a CAPITAL felony is outside it. What does apply to a capital felony lives in s. 775.082(1) and s. 921.141, which were not read.
rows.quote: A person who has been convicted of an offense other than a capital felony may be sentenced to pay a fine in addition to any punishment described in s. 775.082

rows.cite: 775.083(1) (introductory text, second clause -- fine in lieu of punishment)
rows.scope: only where another statute specifically authorizes a fine in lieu of s. 775.082 punishment
rows.trigger: 'IN LIEU OF' FINE AUTHORITY. The default posture is a fine ADDED TO the s. 775.082 punishment. This clause creates a second, materially different posture: a fine that SUBSTITUTES for that punishment, i.e. displaces imprisonment. It is not self-executing -- it is available only 'when specifically authorized by statute,' meaning the charging or penalty statute must itself grant it. Do not assume a fine may replace incarceration under this section alone; check the charging statute. Distinct from paragraph (g), which raises the fine CEILING when another statute authorizes a higher amount; this clause changes what the fine REPLACES.
rows.quote: when specifically authorized by statute, he or she may be sentenced to pay a fine in lieu of any punishment described in s. 775.082.

rows.cite: 775.083(1) (introductory text, second sentence -- noncriminal violation fine authority)
rows.trigger: SEPARATE AUTHORIZING SENTENCE for noncriminal violations, independent of the criminal-conviction sentence that precedes it. It supplies the AUTHORITY to fine a noncriminal violation; paragraph (1)(e) supplies only the CAP ($500, shared with second degree misdemeanors). The prior table reached noncriminal violations only glancingly inside the (1)(e) row and never captured this grant. Note this sentence carries no reference to s. 775.082, because a noncriminal violation has no term of imprisonment to be added to or substituted for.
rows.quote: A person who has been convicted of a noncriminal violation may be sentenced to pay a fine.

rows.cite: 775.083(1) (introductory text, third sentence -- 'shall not exceed' connector)
rows.trigger: CONNECTOR that converts the lettered list into MAXIMA rather than mandatory amounts. The figures in (a) through (g) are ceilings a fine 'shall not exceed'; nothing in this section requires that a fine be imposed at all, or at any floor. Every min field in this table is null for that reason, and no row states a mandatory minimum fine. Also note the connector's own scope words, 'designated crimes and ... noncriminal violations,' which carry the capital-felony exclusion from the first sentence forward into the whole ladder.
rows.quote: Fines for designated crimes and for noncriminal violations shall not exceed:

rows.trigger: Fine cap of $15,000 where the conviction is of a life felony. This paragraph does nothing else; the section-wide caveat formerly attached to this row now sits on the section-level row cited '775.083'. Contrast the capital-felony row: a life felony is covered here, a capital felony is excluded by the lead-in.
rows.quote: $15,000, when the conviction is of a life felony.

rows.trigger: Fine cap of $10,000 where the conviction is of a first degree OR second degree felony. Note both degrees share one cap; do not read this as distinguishing them.
rows.quote: $10,000, when the conviction is of a felony of the first or second degree.

rows.trigger: Fine cap of $5,000 where the conviction is of a third degree felony.
rows.quote: $5,000, when the conviction is of a felony of the third degree.

rows.trigger: Fine cap of $1,000 where the conviction is of a first degree misdemeanor.
rows.quote: $1,000, when the conviction is of a misdemeanor of the first degree.

rows.trigger: Fine cap of $500 where the conviction is of a second degree misdemeanor OR a noncriminal violation. This paragraph is a CAP only; the authority to fine a noncriminal violation comes from the second sentence of the lead-in, rowed separately above.
rows.quote: $500, when the conviction is of a misdemeanor of the second degree or a noncriminal violation.

rows.scope: applies on top of the (a)-(e) ladder; no upper bound

rows.quote: Any higher amount equal to double the pecuniary gain derived from the offense by the offender or double the pecuniary loss suffered by the victim.

rows.scope: applies on top of the (a)-(e) ladder; no upper bound
rows.trigger: SECOND OVERRIDE, uncapped. Any higher amount specifically authorized by any other statute displaces the ladder in (a) through (e). Never state a maximum fine from paragraphs (a) through (e) alone without checking the charging statute for its own authorized amount. Distinguish the lead-in's 'in lieu of' clause, which also turns on specific statutory authorization but changes what the fine replaces rather than how high it may go.
rows.quote: Any higher amount specifically authorized by statute.

rows.trigger: CLOSING unnumbered text of subsection (1) -- the second of the two flush passages in this subsection (the other precedes paragraph (a) and is rowed above). Contains a definition that matters materially: for fine purposes 'convicted'/'conviction' includes a plea of guilty or nolo contendere EVEN WHERE ADJUDICATION IS WITHHELD. Also directs deposit into the s. 142.01 fine and forfeiture fund and permits deferred payment to a date certain where the defendant is unable to pay.
rows.quote: Fines imposed in this subsection shall be deposited by the clerk of the court in the fine and forfeiture fund established pursuant to s. 142.01. If a defendant is unable to pay a fine, the court may defer payment of the fine to a date certain. As used in this subsection, the term "convicted" or "conviction" means a determination of guilt which is the result of a trial or the entry of a plea of guilty or nolo contendere, regardless of whether adjudication is withheld.

rows.scope: felonies, misdemeanors, criminal traffic offenses, delinquency adjudications, and municipal/county ordinance violations constituting misdemeanors under state law
rows.trigger: Mandatory court costs assessed IN ADDITION TO the subsection (1) fines: $50 for a felony, $20 for any other offense. Not a fine cap and not a degree. The quote below is now the COMPLETE subsection -- the prior table cut it mid-sentence at '$20 for any other offense' with no ellipsis, hiding the disposition and use-restriction language: costs are deposited by the clerk into an appropriate county account, the county must account for them separately as crime prevention funds, and the county must expend them, in consultation with the sheriff, on crime prevention programs in the county. Note the contrast with subsection (1) fines, which go to the s. 142.01 fine and forfeiture fund instead.
rows.quote: In addition to the fines set forth in subsection (1), court costs shall be assessed and collected in each instance a defendant pleads nolo contendere to, or is convicted of, or adjudicated delinquent for, a felony, a misdemeanor, or a criminal traffic offense under state law, or a violation of any municipal or county ordinance if the violation constitutes a misdemeanor under state law. The court costs imposed by this section shall be $50 for a felony and $20 for any other offense and shall be deposited by the clerk of the court into an appropriate county account for disbursement for the purposes provided in this subsection. A county shall account for the funds separately from other county funds as crime prevention funds. The county, in consultation with the sheriff, must expend such funds for crime prevention programs in the county.

rows.scope: county handling of collected court costs
rows.trigger: Broken out as its own row so a consumer filtering by cite cannot miss it: the back half of subsection (2) is not about who pays or how much, it is a binding restriction on the COUNTY. Costs go into an appropriate county account, must be accounted for separately from other county funds as crime prevention funds, and MUST be expended on county crime prevention programs, in consultation with the sheriff. 'Must expend' is mandatory, not permissive. Wholly absent from the prior table.
rows.quote: and shall be deposited by the clerk of the court into an appropriate county account for disbursement for the purposes provided in this subsection. A county shall account for the funds separately from other county funds as crime prevention funds. The county, in consultation with the sheriff, must expend such funds for crime prevention programs in the county.

rows.trigger: Procedural only. Clerk of court collects; the person ordered to pay must contact the clerk immediately to pay in full or apply for a s. 28.246(4) payment plan. No degree, no dollar trigger. Read alongside the closing flush text of subsection (1), which separately allows the court to defer a fine to a date certain for inability to pay.
rows.quote: The clerk of the court of each county is the entity responsible for collecting payment of fines, fees, service charges, and court costs. Unless otherwise designated by the court, a person who has been ordered to pay court obligations under this section shall immediately contact the clerk to pay fines, fees, service charges, and court costs in full or to apply for enrollment in a payment plan pursuant to s. 28.246(4).

rows.trigger: Incorporation-by-reference clause. This is WHY hundreds of other Florida offense statutes end with the phrase 'and punished as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084' -- a bare reference to this section pulls in the whole fine schedule, INCLUDING the subsection (1) lead-in limits, so an incorporating statute also inherits the capital-felony exclusion and the in-addition-to default. It confirms 775.083 is a downstream penalty provision, never the source of a degree.
rows.quote: The purpose of this section is to provide uniform penalty authorization for criminal offenses and, to this end, a reference to this section constitutes a general reference under the doctrine of incorporation by reference.

775.084.title: Violent career criminals; habitual felony offenders and habitual violent felony offenders; three-time violent felony offenders; definitions; procedure; enhanced penalties or mandatory minimum prison terms.

rows.trigger: Cross-cutting predicate definition, not a penalty. Defines "qualified offense," the out-of-state/federal/foreign conviction that counts as a predicate. It feeds the (1)(a) habitual felony offender predicate ("two or more felonies in this state or other qualified offenses") and the (1)(d) violent career criminal predicate ("an offense in this state or other qualified offense"), so it silently widens the prior-conviction pool for the (4)(a) and (4)(d) rows. Given its own row rather than being buried in trigger prose because it maps to no single penalty row. Note the substantive limits it carries: elements AND penalties must be substantially similar to a Florida offense, and the foreign offense must have been punishable by death or imprisonment exceeding 1 year at the time of commission.
rows.quote: “Qualified offense” means any offense, substantially similar in elements and penalties to an offense in this state, which is in violation of a law of any other jurisdiction, whether that of another state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any possession or territory thereof, or any foreign jurisdiction, that was punishable under the law of such jurisdiction at the time of its commission by the defendant by death or imprisonment exceeding 1 year.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table entirely. Cross-cutting predicate expansion that governs every penalty row in subsection (4). It is not derivable from the (1)(a)-(1)(d) definitional text, which speaks only of a defendant "previously convicted." A withheld adjudication (probation or community control without an adjudication of guilt) is not a conviction under ordinary Florida usage, and this subsection overrides that for all four categories: habitual felony offender, habitual violent felony offender, three-time violent felony offender, and violent career criminal. It applies "for the purposes of this section," so its reach is the whole section. Read together with (5), which cuts the other way by requiring the priors to have been sentenced separately and sequentially.
rows.quote: For the purposes of this section, the placing of a person on probation or community control without an adjudication of guilt shall be treated as a prior conviction.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: promoted from trigger prose to its own row. Converts the permissive "may sentence" of (4)(a) and (4)(b) into a mandatory sanction for offenses committed on or after October 1, 1995, subject to one escape: the court may decline if it finds the sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public, in which case it must provide written reasons (or a transcript of orally stated reasons filed within 7 days) and the court must report those reasons monthly to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research. Two preconditions gate the mandate: the state attorney must PURSUE the sanction, and the court must find the (1) criteria met in a separate proceeding. Governs all six rows at (4)(a)1.-3. and (4)(b)1.-3. Notably absent for the three-time violent felony offender, see (3)(b)6.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after October 1, 1995, if the state attorney pursues a habitual felony offender sanction or a habitual violent felony offender sanction against the defendant and the court, in a separate proceeding pursuant to this paragraph, determines that the defendant meets the criteria under subsection (1) for imposing such sanction, the court must sentence the defendant as a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender, subject to imprisonment pursuant to this section unless the court finds that such sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: promoted from trigger prose to its own row. The three-time violent felony offender analogue of (3)(a)6., and the critical contrast with it: this subparagraph contains NO protection-of-the-public escape clause, and (4)(e) likewise routes only to paragraph (3)(a) and paragraph (3)(c), never to (3)(b). Once the state attorney pursues the sanction and the court finds the (1)(c) criteria met, the (4)(c)1. mandatory minimums must be imposed. Governs the four rows at (4)(c)1.a.-d.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after the effective date of this act, if the state attorney pursues a three-time violent felony offender sanction against the defendant and the court, in a separate proceeding pursuant to this paragraph, determines that the defendant meets the criteria under subsection (1) for imposing such sanction, the court must sentence the defendant as a three-time violent felony offender, subject to imprisonment pursuant to this section as provided in paragraph (4)(c).

rows.trigger: REPAIR: promoted from trigger prose to its own row. The violent career criminal analogue of (3)(a)6. Mandatory once the state attorney pursues the sanction and the (1)(d) criteria are found, subject to the same protection-of-the-public escape with written reasons, 7-day transcript option, and monthly reporting to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research. Governs the three rows at (4)(d)1.-3. Works in tandem with (4)(e), which supplies the consequence of the escape finding.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after October 1, 1995, if the state attorney pursues a violent career criminal sanction against the defendant and the court, in a separate proceeding pursuant to this paragraph, determines that the defendant meets the criteria under subsection (1) for imposing such sanction, the court must sentence the defendant as a violent career criminal, subject to imprisonment pursuant to this section unless the court finds that such sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table and from every trigger. Post-sentencing review limitation unique to the violent career criminal rows at (4)(d)1.-3. Preserves direct appeal and an any-time illegal-sentence motion by either party, then removes the substance: the trial court's decision to impose OR to decline to impose a violent career criminal sentence is presumed appropriate, and no collateral or postconviction motion may be considered on a claim that the sentence is inappropriate, inadequate, or excessive. Note the presumption runs both directions, so the state is barred from collaterally attacking a declination under (4)(e) just as the defendant is barred from attacking an imposition. Also note (3)(c)3.: violent career criminal findings are "appealable only as provided in paragraph (d)," a narrower review right than the (3)(a)4. and (3)(b)4. findings, which are appealable to the extent normally applicable.
rows.quote: A person sentenced under paragraph (4)(d) as a violent career criminal has the right of direct appeal, and either the state or the defendant may petition the trial court to vacate an illegal sentence at any time. However, the determination of the trial court to impose or not to impose a violent career criminal sentence is presumed appropriate and no petition or motion for collateral or other postconviction relief may be considered based on an allegation either by the state or the defendant that such sentence is inappropriate, inadequate, or excessive.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added. Second limitation on review of violent career criminal sentences, and a separate rule from (3)(d)1. Imposes a 2-year outside limit measured from finality of judgment and sentence on ALL claims of error or illegality, on direct appeal and collateral review alike, unless the basis could not have been ascertained by due diligence. Separately bars appeal by either party of technical violations and mistakes at trial and sentencing that do not affect due process or fundamental fairness. Framed as legislative intent rather than flat prohibition, which is preserved here rather than resolved.
rows.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that, with respect to both direct appeal and collateral review of violent career criminal sentences, all claims of error or illegality be raised at the first opportunity and that no claim should be filed more than 2 years after the judgment and sentence became final, unless it is established that the basis for the claim could not have been ascertained at the time by the exercise of due diligence. Technical violations and mistakes at trials and sentencing proceedings involving violent career criminals that do not affect due process or fundamental fairness are not appealable by either the state or the defendant.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added. Third and last of the (3)(d) restrictions, a funding bar rather than a procedural one, and the one most easily missed because it follows two subparagraphs that both read as review limitations. Directs that no state or political-subdivision funds, resources, or employees be used, directly or indirectly, in appellate or collateral proceedings based on violent career criminal sentencing, except where constitutionally or statutorily mandated. The mandate exception is what preserves appointed appellate counsel in practice.
rows.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that no funds, resources, or employees of the state or its political subdivisions be used, directly or indirectly, in appellate or collateral proceedings based on violent career criminal sentencing, except when such use is constitutionally or statutorily mandated.

rows.trigger: Habitual felony offender whose current offense is a life felony or a felony of the first degree. This section assigns NO degree of offense at all; it prescribes a term directly for an already-graded felony. There is no dollar value anywhere in s. 775.084, so min and max are null on every row, not merely unstated. Eligibility requires the (1)(a) findings: two or more prior felony convictions in this state or other qualified offenses per (1)(e); the new felony committed while serving a sentence or supervision for a prior felony or within 5 years of the last prior conviction or release, whichever is later; neither the new felony nor one of the two priors being an s. 893.13 purchase or possession offense; no pardon; and no prior set aside in postconviction. Predicate counting is further governed by (2) (withheld adjudication counts) and (5) (priors must have been sentenced separately and sequentially before the current offense). Permissive on its face ("may"), but mandatory under (3)(a)6. subject to the protection-of-the-public finding at (4)(e). The term is a ceiling, not a floor. Gain-time eligible under (4)(k)1.; conditional release under (4)(j) applies; not subject to the Criminal Punishment Code per (4)(h); may not be increased after imposition per (4)(g).
rows.quote: In the case of a life felony or a felony of the first degree, for life.

rows.trigger: Habitual felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the second degree. Term prescribed directly; the underlying offense keeps its own degree. No value trigger. Same (1)(a) predicate findings as (4)(a)1., including the (2) withheld-adjudication expansion and the (5) sequential-conviction requirement, and the same (3)(a)6. must-impose rule with the (4)(e) protection-of-the-public escape. The 30 years is a CEILING against an ordinary second degree maximum of 15 years; there is no mandatory minimum in this row. Gain-time eligible under (4)(k)1.; (4)(j) conditional release applies; (4)(g) and (4)(h) apply.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the second degree, for a term of years not exceeding 30.

rows.trigger: Habitual felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the third degree. Term prescribed directly. No value trigger. The 10 years is a CEILING against an ordinary third degree maximum of 5 years; no mandatory minimum. Same (1)(a) predicate as read with (2) and (5), same (3)(a)6. mandate and (4)(e) escape, same (4)(g), (4)(h), (4)(j), and (4)(k)1. consequences.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the third degree, for a term of years not exceeding 10.

rows.trigger: Habitual VIOLENT felony offender whose current offense is a life felony or a felony of the first degree. Requires under (1)(b)1. one or more prior convictions, or an attempt or conspiracy, for an offense on the closed list at (1)(b)1.a.-o.: arson; sexual battery; robbery; kidnapping; aggravated child abuse; aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult; aggravated assault with a deadly weapon; murder; manslaughter; aggravated manslaughter of an elderly person or disabled adult; aggravated manslaughter of a child; unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb; armed burglary; aggravated battery; or aggravated stalking. Plus the (1)(b)2. timing (while serving a sentence or supervision for an enumerated felony, or within 5 years of that conviction or release, whichever is later), (1)(b)3. no pardon on the ground of innocence, and (1)(b)4. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). Mandatory under (3)(a)6. subject to the (4)(e) escape. Adds a 15-year release ineligibility on top of the life term. Gain-time eligible under (4)(k)1., and s. 947.1405 conditional release applies under (4)(j).
rows.quote: In the case of a life felony or a felony of the first degree, for life, and such offender shall not be eligible for release for 15 years.

rows.trigger: Habitual violent felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the second degree. Same (1)(b) enumerated-prior predicate as (4)(b)1., read with (2) and (5). Dual-bound in substance: a 30-year CEILING plus a 10-year release ineligibility, which functions as a floor on time served though it is not phrased as a mandatory minimum term. Mandatory under (3)(a)6. subject to the (4)(e) escape. Gain-time eligible under (4)(k)1.; (4)(j) applies.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the second degree, for a term of years not exceeding 30, and such offender shall not be eligible for release for 10 years.

rows.trigger: Habitual violent felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the third degree. Same (1)(b) enumerated-prior predicate, read with (2) and (5). A 10-year CEILING plus a 5-year release ineligibility. Mandatory under (3)(a)6. subject to the (4)(e) escape. Gain-time eligible under (4)(k)1.; (4)(j) applies.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the third degree, for a term of years not exceeding 10, and such offender shall not be eligible for release for 5 years.

rows.trigger: Three-time violent felony offender where the current felony is punishable by life. MANDATORY MINIMUM, not a ceiling, and the court "must" impose it. There is NO protection-of-the-public escape for this category: (3)(b)6. omits it and (4)(e) routes only to paragraph (3)(a) and paragraph (3)(c). Requires under (1)(c)1. two or more prior adult convictions for felonies or attempts from the list at (1)(c)1.a.-q., which is the (1)(b) list PLUS home invasion/robbery and carjacking, and under (1)(c)1.r. also counts substantially similar out-of-jurisdiction offenses. Under (1)(c)2. the CURRENT felony must itself be one of the offenses enumerated in 1.a.-q. (note: a.-q., not a.-r.) with the same serving-a-sentence or within-5-years timing, though the timing predicates reference the broader a.-r. list. Plus (1)(c)3. no pardon on innocence and (1)(c)4. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). Under (4)(k)3., for offenses on or after July 1, 1999, release only by expiration of sentence, no parole, control release, or any form of early release, which displaces the general gain-time eligibility of (4)(k)1. for this category. The wording "a felony punishable by life" is broader than "life felony" as used in (4)(a), (4)(b), and (4)(d); that ambiguity is preserved here rather than resolved. Not capped by the figure stated: see (4)(c)2., which is a subsection-wide savings clause.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony punishable by life, to a term of imprisonment for life;

rows.trigger: Three-time violent felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the first degree. Mandatory minimum of 30 years, a FLOOR and not a maximum; the (4)(c)2. savings clause preserves a greater sentence. Same (1)(c) predicate read with (2) and (5), and the current offense must itself be an enumerated violent felony under (1)(c)2. No protection-of-the-public escape. Release only by expiration of sentence under (4)(k)3. for offenses on or after July 1, 1999.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the first degree, to a term of imprisonment of 30 years;

rows.trigger: Three-time violent felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the second degree. Mandatory minimum of 15 years, which equals the ordinary statutory maximum for a second degree felony, so it converts that maximum into a floor. A FLOOR, not a ceiling; (4)(c)2. preserves a greater sentence as authorized by law. Same (1)(c) predicate read with (2) and (5). No protection-of-the-public escape. (4)(k)3. release restriction applies.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the second degree, to a term of imprisonment of 15 years; or

rows.trigger: Three-time violent felony offender whose current offense is a felony of the third degree. Mandatory minimum of 5 years, which equals the ordinary third degree maximum, so it converts that maximum into a floor. A FLOOR, not a ceiling; (4)(c)2. preserves a greater sentence. Same (1)(c) predicate read with (2) and (5). No protection-of-the-public escape. (4)(k)3. release restriction applies.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the third degree, to a term of imprisonment of 5 years.

rows.trigger: REPAIR (scope corrected, twice). Not a penalty assignment but a savings clause on sentencing authority. CORRECTION 1: the prior table said this governs "every row in (4)(c)" and was recorded so "the (4)(c) figures are not mistaken for maximums." The text says "Nothing in this SUBSECTION." In Florida statutory hierarchy the subsection is (4) and the paragraph is (c), so this clause reaches ALL of subsection (4), including the (4)(a) habitual felony offender rows, the (4)(b) habitual violent felony offender rows, and the (4)(d) violent career criminal rows, not merely (4)(c). Its placement as subparagraph 2. under paragraph (c) is the trap: the location suggests paragraph scope, the words do not. Read literally it preserves the court's authority to impose a greater sentence of incarceration as authorized by law throughout subsection (4), which matters most where a row states a ceiling (the 30 and 10 of (4)(a), the 30 and 10 of (4)(b), the 40 and 15 of (4)(d)) because "as authorized by law" is what does the limiting work there, not the numbers in the row. CORRECTION 2: scope was "prior"; this provision is not keyed to prior convictions at all and scope is now null.
rows.quote: Nothing in this subsection shall prevent a court from imposing a greater sentence of incarceration as authorized by law.

rows.trigger: Violent career criminal whose current offense is a life felony or a felony of the first degree. Mandatory in form ("shall"), but under (3)(c)5. and (4)(e) the court may decline if it finds in writing that the sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public. Requires under (1)(d)1. three or more prior adult convictions in this state or qualified offenses for: any forcible felony as described in s. 776.08; aggravated stalking under s. 784.048(3) and (4); aggravated child abuse under s. 827.03(2)(a); aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult under s. 825.102(2); lewd or lascivious battery, molestation, conduct, or exhibition under s. 800.04 or s. 847.0135(5); escape under s. 944.40; or a felony violation of chapter 790 involving use or possession of a firearm. PLUS (1)(d)2. prior incarceration in a state or federal prison, PLUS (1)(d)3. the primary offense being an enumerated felony committed on or after October 1, 1995 with the serving-a-sentence or within-5-years timing, PLUS (1)(d)4. no pardon and (1)(d)5. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). Under (4)(k)2. no discretionary early release other than pardon, executive clemency, or conditional medical release under s. 947.149. Review of the sentence, and of a refusal to impose it, is restricted by (3)(c)3. and (3)(d)1.-3. Note (4)(j) does NOT extend s. 947.1405 conditional release to this category; it names only habitual felony offenders and habitual violent felony offenders.
rows.quote: In the case of a life felony or a felony of the first degree, for life.

rows.trigger: Violent career criminal whose current offense is a felony of the second degree. This provision carries BOTH bounds: a 40-year ceiling AND a 30-year mandatory minimum, against an ordinary second degree maximum of 15 years. Because min and max in this schema carry dollar-value semantics and this section states no dollar values, that dual-bound structure lives only in the quote and this trigger; see the unread field, where the schema gap is named. Same (1)(d) three-prior-plus-prior-imprisonment predicate as (4)(d)1., read with (2) and (5). Mandatory under (3)(c)5. subject to the (4)(e) escape. (4)(k)2. release restriction and the (3)(d)1.-3. review restrictions apply.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the second degree, for a term of years not exceeding 40, with a mandatory minimum term of 30 years’ imprisonment.

rows.trigger: Violent career criminal whose current offense is a felony of the third degree. Dual-bound: a 15-year ceiling AND a 10-year mandatory minimum, against an ordinary third degree maximum of 5 years. Same (1)(d) predicate read with (2) and (5). Mandatory under (3)(c)5. subject to the (4)(e) escape. (4)(k)2. release restriction and the (3)(d)1.-3. review restrictions apply.
rows.quote: In the case of a felony of the third degree, for a term of years not exceeding 15, with a mandatory minimum term of 10 years’ imprisonment.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added as a row; the prior table mentioned it only in passing inside the (4)(d)1. trigger. The protection-of-the-public override, and the provision that supplies the CONSEQUENCE of the finding described in (3)(a)6. and (3)(c)5.: the sentence is imposed without regard to this section entirely, meaning the defendant is sentenced under the ordinary guidelines and statutory maximums with no enhancement, not merely at a lower enhanced figure. Reaches habitual felony offenders, habitual violent felony offenders, AND violent career criminals, so it governs the nine rows at (4)(a)1.-3., (4)(b)1.-3., and (4)(d)1.-3., not only the violent career criminal rows. It does NOT reach three-time violent felony offenders: it routes only to paragraph (3)(a) and paragraph (3)(c), never (3)(b), which is why the four (4)(c)1. rows have no escape. Limited to offenses committed on or after October 1, 1995.
rows.quote: If the court finds, pursuant to paragraph (3)(a) or paragraph (3)(c), that it is not necessary for the protection of the public to sentence a defendant who meets the criteria for sentencing as a habitual felony offender, a habitual violent felony offender, or a violent career criminal, with respect to an offense committed on or after October 1, 1995, sentence shall be imposed without regard to this section.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table. Duty-to-determine provision governing all thirteen penalty rows. Whenever it APPEARS to the court that the defendant is eligible under this section, the court shall make the determination through the separate proceeding at (3)(a), (3)(b), or (3)(c) as applicable. Phrased as a court obligation triggered by apparent eligibility, and it is not conditioned on the state attorney pursuing the sanction, unlike the must-impose rules at (3)(a)6., (3)(b)6., and (3)(c)5., which are. The tension between the two is preserved here rather than resolved.
rows.quote: At any time when it appears to the court that the defendant is eligible for sentencing under this section, the court shall make that determination as provided in paragraph (3)(a), paragraph (3)(b), or paragraph (3)(c).

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table. One-way ratchet limiting all thirteen penalty rows: a sentence imposed under this section shall not be increased after imposition. Bars upward correction on resentencing or on state appeal. Read against (4)(c)2., which permits a greater sentence at the time of imposition but not after it, and against (3)(d)1., which lets either party move to vacate an ILLEGAL sentence at any time.
rows.quote: A sentence imposed under this section shall not be increased after such imposition.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table. This is the provision that actually controls the null "level" field on every row in this table. A sentence imposed under s. 775.084 is not subject to s. 921.002, the Criminal Punishment Code, so the offense-severity-level machinery, the lowest permissible sentence computation, and the departure rules do not apply to these sentences. The prior table justified null levels by reasoning that 775.084 creates no ranked offense; that reasoning is correct as far as it goes, but this paragraph is the operative text and it is now cited. Governs all thirteen penalty rows.
rows.quote: A sentence imposed under this section is not subject to s. 921.002.

rows.trigger: REPAIR (scope corrected from "prior" to "current"). Not a penalty assignment but an offense-class exclusion keyed to the CURRENT offense, not to any prior conviction: none of the s. 775.084 enhancements reach capital felonies, and being sentenced under this section does not preclude imposition of the death penalty for a capital felony. Bounds every penalty row above. Recorded because a table of the subsection (4) penalties alone would wrongly imply the section covers the top of the felony ladder. Note the interaction with (4)(c)1.a., which reaches "a felony punishable by life": that phrase stops short of capital felonies by force of this paragraph.
rows.quote: The provisions of this section do not apply to capital felonies, and a sentence authorized under this section does not preclude the imposition of the death penalty for a capital felony.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table. Attaches s. 947.1405 conditional release supervision to persons sentenced as habitual felony offenders and as habitual violent felony offenders, that is, to the six rows at (4)(a)1.-3. and (4)(b)1.-3. It does NOT name three-time violent felony offenders or violent career criminals, and that omission is load-bearing: it aligns with the (4)(k)2. and (4)(k)3. release restrictions, which foreclose discretionary early release for those two categories. A downstream consumer reading only the (4)(a) and (4)(b) terms would miss that release from those terms carries a post-release supervision tail.
rows.quote: The provisions of s. 947.1405 shall apply to persons sentenced as habitual felony offenders and persons sentenced as habitual violent felony offenders.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; this is the exact failure pattern the repair exists to catch. The prior table picked up (4)(k)2. and (4)(k)3. inside trigger prose and dropped subparagraph 1. of the same paragraph, because 2. and 3. answered the question being asked (what release restrictions attach to violent career criminals and three-time offenders) and 1. did not. Subparagraph 1. is the affirmative grant that runs the other way: a defendant sentenced under this section as a habitual felony offender, a habitual violent felony offender, OR a violent career criminal is ELIGIBLE for gain-time under s. 944.275(4)(b). It reaches all three of those categories, so it applies to the nine rows at (4)(a)1.-3., (4)(b)1.-3., and (4)(d)1.-3., and it materially changes actual time served on every one of them. For violent career criminals it must be read against (4)(k)2., which forecloses discretionary early release but does not by its terms strip the (4)(k)1. gain-time eligibility; that tension is preserved rather than resolved. Note that three-time violent felony offenders are the one category NOT named in subparagraph 1., consistent with the absolute expiration-of-sentence rule in (4)(k)3.
rows.quote: A defendant sentenced under this section as a habitual felony offender, a habitual violent felony offender, or a violent career criminal is eligible for gain-time granted by the Department of Corrections as provided in s. 944.275(4)(b).

rows.trigger: REPAIR: promoted from trigger prose to its own row. Release restriction specific to violent career criminals, governing the three rows at (4)(d)1.-3. For offenses committed on or after October 1, 1995, no form of discretionary early release, with three carve-outs: pardon, executive clemency, and conditional medical release granted pursuant to s. 947.149. Narrower than the (4)(k)3. three-time offender rule, which admits no carve-outs at all.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after October 1, 1995, a defendant sentenced under this section as a violent career criminal is not eligible for any form of discretionary early release, other than pardon or executive clemency, or conditional medical release granted pursuant to s. 947.149.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: promoted from trigger prose to its own row. The most absolute release restriction in the section, governing the four rows at (4)(c)1.a.-d. For offenses committed on or after July 1, 1999, a three-time violent felony offender is released ONLY by expiration of sentence: no parole, no control release, no form of early release, and no pardon or clemency carve-out of the kind (4)(k)2. gives violent career criminals. Consistent with the omission of three-time violent felony offenders from the (4)(k)1. gain-time grant and from the (4)(j) conditional release provision.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after July 1, 1999, a defendant sentenced under this section as a three-time violent felony offender shall be released only by expiration of sentence and shall not be eligible for parole, control release, or any form of early release.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; absent from the prior table and from every trigger in it. The sequential-conviction requirement, a hard predicate limit on all thirteen penalty rows and the most heavily litigated eligibility rule in the section. To be counted as a prior felony under this section the felony must have (a) resulted in a conviction, (b) been sentenced separately PRIOR to the current offense, and (c) been sentenced separately from any other felony conviction being counted as a prior. Its practical effect is that multiple felonies disposed of at a single sentencing hearing collapse into one countable prior, and priors sentenced after the commission of the current offense do not count at all. It governs the (1)(a) two-or-more count, the (1)(b) one-or-more count, the (1)(c) two-or-more count, and the (1)(d) three-or-more count alike. Cuts against (2), which expands the prior-conviction pool to withheld adjudications; (5) then subtracts from that pool by requiring separate sequential sentencing.
rows.quote: In order to be counted as a prior felony for purposes of sentencing under this section, the felony must have resulted in a conviction sentenced separately prior to the current offense and sentenced separately from any other felony conviction that is to be counted as a prior felony.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added. Purpose and construction clause, and it is operative rather than hortatory: it declares that a reference to this section constitutes a GENERAL reference under the doctrine of incorporation by reference, which means statutes elsewhere that cross-reference s. 775.084 pick up its later amendments automatically rather than freezing the text as of the referencing statute's enactment. Recorded because a table of the penalty rows alone gives a downstream consumer no signal that this section's amendments propagate outward through every statute that cites it.
rows.quote: The purpose of this section is to provide uniform punishment for those crimes made punishable under this section, and to this end, a reference to this section constitutes a general reference under the doctrine of incorporation by reference.

unread: READING METHOD, stated so the coverage claim can be checked: raw HTML fetched by curl from https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/775.084, stripped to text locally, and read line by line start to finish, not summarized by a model. Every subsection, paragraph, subparagraph, and sub-subparagraph of the section was read: (1)(a)1.-5., (1)(b)1.a.-o. and 2.-4., (1)(c)1.a.-r. and 2.-4., (1)(d)1.a.-g. and 2.-5., (1)(e), (2), (3)(a)1.-6., (3)(b)1.-6., (3)(c)1.-5., (3)(d)1.-3., (4)(a)1.-3. through (4)(k)1.-3., (5), (6), and the History note.

(1)(a)1.-5., (1)(b)1.a.-o. and 2.-4., (1)(c)1.a.-r. and 2.-4., and (1)(d)1.a.-g. and 2.-5. are the four category definitions; each maps one-to-one onto the penalty rows it gates and is recited in full inside those rows' triggers, so duplicating it as a row would double-count. The cross-cutting predicate rules that map to NO single penalty row -- (1)(e), (2), and (5) -- were given their own rows precisely because that rule does not cover them.

READ BUT NOT GIVEN A ROW, pure procedure: (3)(a)1.-5. (presentence investigation, written notice, open court with confrontation and counsel, preponderance standard and appealability, fingerprinting under s. 921.241), (3)(b)1.-5. (the same five for three-time violent felony offenders), and (3)(c)1.-4. (the same, minus any presentence investigation requirement, and with findings appealable ONLY as provided in (3)(d)). Two substantive asymmetries inside these otherwise parallel lists are recorded here rather than lost: (3)(c) contains NO presentence-investigation requirement while (3)(a)1. and (3)(b)1. both do, and (3)(c)3. narrows appellate review of violent career criminal findings to (3)(d) while (3)(a)4. and (3)(b)4. leave findings appealable to the extent normally applicable.

Any consumer computing exposure from this table must parse the quote.

s. 921.0022 offense severity ranking chart -- NOT opened. Every level is null rather than guessed. Note this is now independently justified by the operative text: (4)(h) provides that a sentence imposed under this section is not subject to s. 921.002, so the Criminal Punishment Code severity-level machinery does not reach these sentences at all; any level would attach to the underlying felony, not to these provisions.

s. 776.08 (definition of forcible felony), incorporated by reference at (1)(d)1.a. -- NOT opened. It materially controls the scope of the three violent career criminal rows at (4)(d)1.-3. and cannot be resolved from the text of 775.084 alone.

s. 893.13 (purchase or possession of a controlled substance), which at (1)(a)3. disqualifies both the current offense and one of the two priors from counting toward habitual felony offender status -- NOT opened. It bounds all three (4)(a) rows.
